The stacking game genre is oriented for realtime play. Temporal mechanics play a
significant role in such games. However, Voat is not well suited to mechanics which
are based on short time intervals due to limitations designed to prevent abuse.

An obvious approach is to make the mechanics turn based. While this eliminates the
pressure of user response time it also expands the strategic dimension, as more
time is allowed for the consideration of player actions. This opens the door to
having a bit more complex gameplay (soaking up some of the boredom of downtime).

Rather than have players wait for each individual movement / rotation / etc. to be
processed prior to displaying the next game state I've designed the graphics to
handle up to 6 consecutive inputs or 7 grid states (not counting line clear).

The initial display of the grid counts as one state, the remaining 6 frames can
render player actions. This makes a total of 128 CSS states. I've reduced this to
64 rules by encoding the initial cell visibility toggle outside the animation rules.

While implementing game logic I decided I'd like to add a new mechanic to the genre
of tetromino shape stacking games. I think I can achieve it with only one more
CSS animation state. However, this will double the amount of CSS rules required.
To keep from expanding CSS size I could instead reduce the max number of moves
per turn to be 5 instead of 6, but this is undesirable.

Six inputs per batch was selected because this is the minimum number of moves needed
to drop an i shape along the furthest columns of the game grid. Any less than six
would leave players hanging while they wait for the next turn to perform the drop
operation and complete the max 4 lines. That would be terrible for game flow, IMO.

Unless I can figure out a "cheap" way to add an 8th frame of cell animation to the
grid (without doubling CSS size) I may have to scrap plans for adding the new
mechanic. I'll have to experiment with encoding the animations and etc. states to
discover if a more compressed representation exists that can yield similar results.

The current batch of 64 independent rules was used because it has better performance
than other approaches. I may have to accept the performance hit in order to squeeze
in more gameplay than the bog standard stacking game.

p.s. Excuse the code-style text. It's needed to bypass current CSS rules and show
the same text with and without custom CSS enabled. I'll fix the CSS rules later.
Adapting Realtime gameplay to the Voat platform

I've ruled out using the animation-fill property to extend the state as this would rely on the initial state, and in 50% of cases the initial state would be different than the desired outcome state. Some shenanigans with "before" can be done to attain 75% coverage of states without creating additional animation rules, but 100% coverage is essential.

It does not appear to be possible to affect one state (such as opacity) via multiple CSS animations. However, visibility may be a potential vector to investigate. Optimally I would have liked each individual frame of the animation to be chained selectively by CSS rules rather than the entire series of states to have to exist in one animation pattern. This is not doable as the first animation rule will override successive changes to the state in the same time period. One can have the states take place one after the other, but if the states are encoded individually as on or off for a duration then this increases CSS size due to the verbosity required to specify each successive state's properties.

Increasing the number of CSS animations to 128 from 64 is seeming like the best option presently. For some reason chaining CSS animations causes odd timing interval discrepancies, where the animations do not happen simultaneously even when scheduled to occur at the same millisecond.

However, there are still some areas to investigate with combinatoric CSS animations. Front end research continues as I nail down back end logic.
